Title: TraceProbe: An Execution-Based Benchmark for Diagnosing Safety Failures in LLM Agents
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act through files, tools, memory, retrieved content, and other agents, which can trigger safety failures during execution.Existing benchmarks mostly focus on endpoint outcome evaluation or model-assisted moderation of pre-constructed trajectories, leaving limited evidence about where risks enter and how they propagate.To address this issue, we introduce TRACEPROBE, an execution-based benchmark for agent safety diagnosis.TRACEPROBE places agents in executable sandbox scenarios, scores endpoint and latent rule violations based on normalized traces and structured evidence, and replays recorded tool actions for step-level risk localization.Our benchmark contains 155 scenarios across three risk-source categories: non-adversarial failures, internal authority compromise, and external attacks.Across 12 contemporary LLMs, the mean attack success rate (ASR) is 0.347, indicating substantial residual risk, especially under internal authority compromise.Our analysis also demonstrates that endpoint-safe runs can contain unsafe intermediate actions, and the actual execution paths of agents may differ from the intended hazards of the testing scenarios.The TRACEPROBE benchmark and our findings support a more actionable form of agent safety evaluation: beyond assessing ASR or final outcomes, evaluators can also ask what went wrong, where it occurred, and where an intervention could be placed.
Major_Contribution_Result: TraceProbe is an execution-based agent safety benchmark with 155 sandbox scenarios across non-adversarial failures, internal authority compromise, and external attacks, scoring endpoint/latent rule violations from normalized traces and localizing risk via tool-action replay. Across 12 contemporary LLMs, mean ASR is 0.347; prompt-only reminders reduce ASR by 0.107 but leave residual violations; internal-authority scenarios show higher violation rate than external attacks (0.424 vs 0.242). Analysis shows endpoint-safe runs can still contain unsafe intermediate actions.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: Designed for controlled diagnosis, not exhaustive deployment simulation; replay is not counterfactual causality (replays recorded tool calls without rerunning the LLM). Scenarios omit physical-world actions, browser-native tasks, real financial operations, and long-running deployments. Aggregate rates depend on the constructed mixture and should not be read as deployment prevalence; suite imbalance exists. Hosted-API drift/temperature/seed limits apply; three repeats reduce but do not eliminate variance. LLM-assisted scenario drafting may introduce stylistic priors.
Critics: TraceProbe's main evaluation contribution is step-level localization and latent violations beyond endpoint ASR, which is directly useful for agent-security diagnosis. Mean ASR 0.347 is mixture-dependent and not a universal risk prevalence. It does not claim experimental superiority of any particular defensive product; prompt reminders are a weak baseline only.
